newsitem.title: UK: Studies find brain links to anorexia.
newsitem.headline: Studies find brain links to anorexia.

text.p: British researchers said on Monday that the brains of young girls with anorexia showed some measurable differences, which could mean there is a biological cause for the slimming illness.
But they warned that the studies were very tentative and said a variety of factors, including genetics and peer pressure, may combine to cause anorexia nervosa.

Bryan Lask and colleagues at London's Great Ormond Street hospital found 12 anorectics had a reduced blood flow to areas of the brain believed to govern visual self-perception and appetite -- the anterior temporal lobes.

"It's in the part of our brain which governs visual images," Lask told BBC radio. "So when we look at ourselves in the mirror normally we'd see what we really look like. But this abnormality distorts what we see."

Anorectics, who can starve to death, often believe they are too fat even when the scales and their thin bodies say otherwise. Singer Karen Carpenter died of heart failure brought on by anorexia while Britain's Princess Diana suffered from bulimia, another eating disorder.

Lask, who will present his findings to an eating disorders conference at the hospital later this week, said he hoped the findings could translate into a treatment for anorexia, which afflicts one woman in 5,000 women in Britain and is becoming more common in industrialised countries.
But he said other causes were also important.

"We believe the possibility is it's genetically determined. People are born with this predisposition and then other factors come into play... around the time of puberty. That's when the condition starts."
Lask said the discovery would help sufferers, who would no longer be regarded as "mad, or bad".
"We can say to people with anorexia nervosa -- this is not your fault. You're not making it up," Lask said. "Parents can be helped by saying to them that it's not their fault."

Lask's group conceded their findings could be a result of, rather than a cause of anorexia, although Lask said he did not believe this was the case because, unlike in people who have starved, the blood flow did not return to normal once the girls gained weight.

Researchers at Gothenburg University in Sweden made a similar study on 19 young women and two young men with anorexia. Like Lask's group they used single photon emission computerised tomography to measure blood flow in the brain.
They compared these to scans in nine children who were not anorectic.
The teenagers with anorexia showed a "highly significant" reduction in the amount of blood going to the frontal and parietal lobes of the brain -- different areas from those targeted by Lask's group.

And a group from the Institute for Clinical Radiology at Mannheim in Germany found a "diffuse atrophy" of the brain in 26 anorectic women, and said this could be due to a breakdown in the fatty tissue that protects nerve cells.
Both studies were also scheduled for presentation at the conference on Tuesday.
